opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to how I like to know whether I'm right.

I was drawn to psychology and economics first because I care about the questions they ask: why people make the choices they do, how incentives shape behavior, how groups coordinate. Those questions still fascinate me. But the more I studied them, the more I felt uneasy about how slowly and indirectly you get feedback. In psychology you run a study, the effect is noisy, and a few years later you're not sure it replicates. In economics you build an elegant model, but the assumptions doing the real work are hard to test against the world. I often couldn't tell whether my reasoning was actually good or just persuasive.

Computer science felt different almost immediately. You write something, you run it, and it either works or it doesn't. The machine doesn't care how confident you sound. That tight loop between idea, implementation, and result really suits me. I think best by building things and poking at them, not by arguing in the abstract for a long time.

It's also constructive. In the social sciences you mostly observe and explain a system that already exists. In CS you get to make the system. If I have a hypothesis about how learning or decision-making might work, I can build a small version and watch it behave. That's still the closest I've found to a laboratory for the questions I originally cared about.

So I don't see it as leaving psychology or economics behind. I see it as finding a toolset that matches my temperament: concrete, iterative, honest with you about when you're wrong. A lot of the most interesting work in AI now loops right back to those old questions about minds, incentives, and behavior. I just get to approach them by building.

r001.rationale: The response says psychology offered slow, indirect, noisy feedback and left Kay unsure whether findings replicated or reasoning was sound.

r002.rationale: It links CS to concrete, hands-on work: writing and running programs, building systems, and testing ideas through their behavior.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts observing and explaining existing systems with building systems, but does not distinguish understanding the world from knowing what one wants to do in it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to how you get to be certain about something. In psychology and economics, I always felt like I was arguing with a very well-read person who could never quite be proven wrong. You build a model of human behavior, and then the data comes in messy, and you tell a story about why the model still kind of holds. There are so many layers between what you think and what the world actually does. That bothered me. Not because the questions weren't interesting, honestly they're more interesting than most of what I work on now, but because the feedback loop was so slow and so negotiable.

Computer science has this quality where the thing you build either works or it doesn't. You write the code, you run it, and the machine gives you an answer with no regard for your feelings or your reputation. When I was a student I found that almost relieving. If I was wrong, I found out in seconds, not in a review cycle two years later. And the reason I was wrong was usually discoverable. I could trace it. I could go line by line and find the exact place where my thinking departed from reality.

The other piece is that I like building things more than I like describing things. Psychology and economics are, at least the way they were taught to me, mostly descriptive disciplines. You observe, you explain. In computer science, the explanation is the artifact. You understand a problem by constructing something that solves it, and if your understanding is incomplete, the construction falls apart in your hands. That matched how my brain already worked. I never really learned anything by reading about it. I learned by trying to make it and watching where it broke.

I'll say, though, I haven't fully left those fields behind. A lot of what's interesting now in AI is essentially psychology and economics coming back in through the side door. How do systems form preferences, how do agents allocate scarce resources, how do incentives shape behavior. So maybe the honest answer is that I didn't choose computer science over those subjects. I chose a toolset where I could finally test the ideas instead of just debating them.

r001.rationale: The response says psychology and economics had many layers between an idea and what the world does, making conclusions indirect and hard to verify.

r002.rationale: It links choosing computer science to building things and understanding problems by constructing solutions.

r003.rationale: The response discusses testing ideas and building things, but does not distinguish understanding the world from knowing what one wants to do in it.

astra-6.text: For me, it was the way computer science let me make an idea concrete. I could break a problem down, write something, and see whether it behaved the way I expected. If it didn’t, I could work through why and try again. That cycle really suited my way of thinking. Psychology and economics ask fascinating questions, but I was more drawn to building something and getting that direct feedback.

r001.rationale: The response values computer science’s direct feedback, but does not say psychology felt too indirect for getting to the bottom of questions.

r002.rationale: It connects the preference to breaking problems down, building something, and seeing whether it works.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish understanding the world from knowing what one wants to do in it.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, computer science offered a more direct way to test my thinking. You could take an idea, turn it into something concrete, and see whether it worked. If it didn’t, you could examine your assumptions and try again. I liked that feedback loop.

Psychology and economics ask fascinating questions, but I found myself more drawn to building things than to explaining human behavior. Computer science gave me a way to break a complicated problem into smaller pieces and work through them. That process felt like a natural fit.

r001.rationale: The candidate says computer science offered a direct way to test ideas, but does not say psychology felt like an indirect route to getting to the bottom of questions.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes turning ideas into concrete things, building, and breaking problems into smaller pieces to work through them.

r003.rationale: The candidate contrasts building things with explaining human behavior, but does not distinguish understanding the world from knowing what one wants to do in it.
